claims.text: A breakpoint suspends the run just before the marked line is executed, and while the run is suspended the debugger can show the values of the variables in scope at that point.
claims.source_hint: .NET / editor debugger documentation, breakpoints: execution is suspended before the marked statement runs; locals and watch windows read the current values

claims.text: Stepping advances a suspended run one statement at a time, suspending it again after each one.
claims.source_hint: .NET / editor debugger documentation, navigate code: step over / step into advance one statement and break again

claims.text: A conditional breakpoint suspends the run only on the passes where its attached condition evaluates to true; on the other passes execution continues without stopping.
claims.source_hint: .NET / editor debugger documentation, breakpoint conditions: conditional expression — break only when the expression is true

claims.text: A breakpoint placed on a statement inside a loop body is never hit when the loop's condition is false on its first evaluation, because the body never executes.
claims.source_hint: C# language reference, the for statement (condition evaluated before each iteration, including the first); breakpoint semantics as in claim 1

claims.text: At stage-0, WrongTotal.TotalVnd loops with `i < lines.Count - 1`, so for the two-item order in WrongTotal.Run the body runs exactly once, with `i` equal to 0, and the second item is never added.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Debug/WrongTotal.cs lines 7-23

claims.text: At stage-0 the order used by both Debug samples is one unit at 1.250.000 and two units at 450.000, written as `{ (1, 1_250_000), (2, 450_000) }`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: WrongTotal.cs line 20 and LoggingDemo.cs line 24

claims.text: At stage-0, Program.cs maps the argument `logging-demo` to LoggingDemo.Run, so `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- logging-demo` runs that sample; the part after `--` selects it.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: samples/DonHang.Samples/Program.cs lines 8 and 23

claims.text: That run prints exactly three lines: `[total] called with 2 lines`, `[total] after line 0: 1250000`, `[total] returning 1250000`.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: LoggingDemo.cs lines 10, 16 and 19 evaluated for the input on line 24; verify by running the sample (no captured output file exists for it)

claims.text: The logging lines live in LoggingDemo.cs, a separate file; WrongTotal.cs at stage-0 contains no Console.WriteLine inside TotalVnd.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: WrongTotal.cs lines 7-16 against LoggingDemo.cs lines 8-21

claims.text: LoggingDemo.cs writes three kinds of line and each carries a value: the count of items received, the running total after each pass, and the value returned.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: LoggingDemo.cs lines 10, 16, 19

claims.text: With `lines.Count` equal to 3 the condition `i < lines.Count - 1` lets `i` take 0 and 1 and then stops, so TotalVnd prints two `[total] after line` lines and never adds the third item.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: LoggingDemo.cs lines 13-17; C# language reference, the for statement

claims.text: The example repository's captured outputs are produced by a machine that runs every script and fails when the output differs from the saved one, so a run there is not one anybody watches.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: STAGE.md, 'CI runs every script and fails if any captured output differs'

claims.text: Opinion: a value watched at a line while the run is suspended is evidence, and the same value concluded by reading the code is not, because reading uses the assumption that may be the bug.
claims.source_hint: outline item 4 of foundation.l2.debugger-and-logging

claims.text: Opinion: logging is the only tool left when you cannot suspend the run — a machine you cannot attach to, an unattended run, a failure that already happened; when you can start or attach to the program the debugger answers without editing the file, though a print may still be quicker.
claims.source_hint: outline item 2 of foundation.l2.debugger-and-logging; review 2026-09-21, claim 14 rephrased

claims.text: Opinion: log the inputs a function received and the decisions it took, with their values, not the bare fact that execution reached a point — where something throws the stack trace already names the path, and where nothing throws "got here" carries no value to compare against.
claims.source_hint: outline item 2 of foundation.l2.debugger-and-logging; review 2026-09-21, claim 15 rephrased

claims.text: Opinion: prints added by hand are acceptable when removed once the question is answered; left in, they print on every call and crowd out the lines that carry information.
claims.source_hint: outline item 3 of foundation.l2.debugger-and-logging

claims.text: Opinion: reach for a conditional breakpoint once a plain one would stop more often than your hypothesis needs; having to skip a breakpoint many times means the case has not been narrowed yet.
claims.source_hint: outline item 1 of foundation.l2.debugger-and-logging

claims.text: Opinion: put the breakpoint on the statement inside the loop body rather than on the `for` statement, because the body's values are what the hypothesis is about and a body that never runs is itself the answer.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: WrongTotal.cs lines 10-13

claims.text: A stack trace carries the exception type, the message and the call sites with file and line, and usually not the value that was wrong at a line; argument exceptions come closest — the message names the parameter, and ArgumentOutOfRangeException exposes the value through its ActualValue property.
claims.source_hint: .NET API reference: Exception.StackTrace, ArgumentNullException message, ArgumentOutOfRangeException ActualValue; examples/don-hang stage-0, output of scripts/debug/run-throws-deep.sh

claims.text: LoggingDemo.TotalVnd writes one call line, one line per loop pass and one return line, so an order of n items prints n + 1 lines: three for the two-item order, four for a three-item one.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang at stage-0: LoggingDemo.cs lines 10, 16, 19 with the loop condition on line 13; C# language reference, the for statement

claims.text: With a breakpoint set only on the adding statement, resuming after its single hit does not suspend the run again — the loop condition is false and the method returns — so reaching the `return` line requires stepping.
claims.source_hint: .NET / editor debugger documentation: continue runs until the next breakpoint is hit, while step commands stop at the next statement; claim 5 for the single hit

claims.text: A breakpoint is set in the editor by clicking the margin beside the line number, and it takes effect on runs started from that editor in debug mode; it is not a change to the source file.
claims.source_hint: .NET debugging tutorial, 'Set a breakpoint' and 'Start debugging': click the left margin of the code window beside the line numbers, then start the program in Debug mode from the editor
